items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the tendency of water to move into the blood by osmosis because of plasma proteins (a lower water potential in plasma)"?
items.answer: Oncotic pressure
items.markingKey: Oncotic pressure: the tendency of water to move into the blood by osmosis because of plasma proteins (a lower water potential in plasma).

items.stem: Explain how tissue fluid is formed and returned to the blood.
items.answer: At arterial end hydrostatic pressure > oncotic pressure, so plasma (water and small solutes) forced out through gaps in capillary walls; at venous end hydrostatic pressure falls below oncotic pressure, so water returns by osmosis; excess drains into lymph.
items.markingKey: any 4 from: At arterial end hydrostatic pressure > oncotic pressure; so plasma (water and small solutes) forced out through gaps in capillary walls; at venous end hydrostatic pressure falls below oncotic pressure; so water returns by osmosis; excess drains into lymph (1 mark each) [4]

items.stem: Explain why the blood pressure falls as blood flows from arteries through capillaries to veins.
items.answer: Friction with vessel walls and the large total cross-sectional area / resistance of arterioles and capillaries; fluid also leaves at capillaries.
items.markingKey: Friction with vessel walls and the large total cross-sectional area / resistance of arterioles and capillaries [1]; fluid also leaves at capillaries [1] [2]

items.stem: In a capillary in the leg, the hydrostatic pressure is 4.1 kPa at the arterial end and 1.5 kPa at the venous end. The oncotic pressure due to plasma proteins is 3.1 kPa along the whole capillary. (a) Calculate the net pressure at each end and state the direction of fluid movement. (b) Explain why the oncotic pressure stays almost the same along the capillary.
items.answer: (a) Arterial end: 1 kPa outwards (fluid leaves); venous end: 1.6 kPa inwards (fluid returns). (b) Plasma proteins are too large to pass through the capillary wall, so their concentration in the blood stays high.
items.markingKey: (a) 4.1 − 3.1 = 1 kPa out [1]; 3.1 − 1.5 = 1.6 kPa in [1]; directions [1] (b) proteins too large to leave [1] [4]

items.stem: In a capillary in the leg, the hydrostatic pressure is 4.6 kPa at the arterial end and 1.8 kPa at the venous end. The oncotic pressure due to plasma proteins is 3.0 kPa along the whole capillary. (a) Calculate the net pressure at each end and state the direction of fluid movement. (b) Explain why the oncotic pressure stays almost the same along the capillary. (c) Explain why less fluid returns to the capillary than leaves it, and what happens to the excess.
items.answer: (a) Arterial end: 1.6 kPa outwards (fluid leaves); venous end: 1.2 kPa inwards (fluid returns). (b) Plasma proteins are too large to pass through the capillary wall, so their concentration in the blood stays high. (c) The net inward pressure is smaller / acts over less time; the excess tissue fluid drains into lymph vessels and is returned to the blood.
items.markingKey: (a) 4.6 − 3.0 = 1.6 kPa out [1]; 3.0 − 1.8 = 1.2 kPa in [1]; directions [1] (b) proteins too large to leave [1] (c) not all returns [1]; drains into lymph [1] [6]

items.stem: A doctor in Seoul sees a patient with swollen ankles (oedema) caused by a blocked lymph vessel caused by the parasite that causes elephantiasis. (a) Explain how this cause leads to the build-up of tissue fluid. (b) Explain how valves in veins help return blood to the heart.
items.answer: (a) Excess tissue fluid cannot drain into the lymph, so it accumulates. (b) Contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes veins; valves allow flow only towards the heart, preventing backflow.
items.markingKey: (a) Excess tissue fluid cannot drain into the lymph [1]; so it accumulates [1] [2] (b) Contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes veins [1]; valves allow flow only towards the heart, preventing backflow [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the structure of a capillary is adapted for exchange.
items.answer: Wall one cell thick (short diffusion distance); pores between cells; narrow lumen so red cells pass slowly and close to wall; extensive networks give large surface area.
items.markingKey: any 3 from: Wall one cell thick (short diffusion distance); pores between cells; narrow lumen so red cells pass slowly and close to wall; extensive networks give large surface area (1 mark each) [3]

items.stem: Nadia says: "Veins always carry deoxygenated blood." Explain whether Nadia is correct.
items.answer: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood; veins are defined by carrying blood to the heart.

items.stem: Compare the structure of an artery and a capillary, and relate each difference to the function of the vessel.
items.answer: Artery: thick wall with much elastic tissue and smooth muscle; narrow lumen; no valves (except at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery); it carries blood away from the heart at high pressure; elastic recoil smooths flow. Capillary: wall one cell thick (endothelium only), with gaps between cells; lumen about 7 μm, just wide enough for a red blood cell; it allows exchange of substances between blood and tissue fluid over a short diffusion distance.
items.markingKey: three structural differences [3]; each linked to function [1] [4]

items.stem: Describe the structures of arteries, veins and capillaries and explain how tissue fluid is formed and returned.
items.answer: Arteries: thick elastic / muscle walls, narrow lumen, high pressure. Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves. Capillaries: one-cell endothelium, exchange. Tissue fluid: hydrostatic vs oncotic pressure at arterial and venous ends; lymph.
items.markingKey: three vessels [3]; formation [2]; return / lymph [2] [7]

items.stem: A doctor in Madrid sees a patient with swollen ankles (oedema) caused by a blocked lymph vessel caused by the parasite that causes elephantiasis. (a) Explain how this cause leads to the build-up of tissue fluid. (b) State the role of the lymphatic system. (c) Explain how valves in veins help return blood to the heart.
items.answer: (a) Excess tissue fluid cannot drain into the lymph, so it accumulates. (b) Drains excess tissue fluid and returns it to the blood near the heart (subclavian veins). (c) Contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes veins; valves allow flow only towards the heart, preventing backflow.
items.markingKey: (a) Excess tissue fluid cannot drain into the lymph [1]; so it accumulates [1] [2] (b) Drains excess tissue fluid and returns it to the blood near the heart (subclavian veins) [2] [2] (c) Contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes veins [1]; valves allow flow only towards the heart, preventing backflow [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the name for "the decrease in the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen at high carbon dioxide concentrations, shifting the dissociation curve to the right"?
items.answer: Bohr shift
items.markingKey: Bohr shift: the decrease in the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen at high carbon dioxide concentrations, shifting the dissociation curve to the right.

items.stem: Explain the role of the chloride shift.
items.answer: HCO₃⁻ formed inside red cells diffuses out into plasma; Cl⁻ moves in to maintain electrical neutrality (balance of charge).
items.markingKey: HCO₃⁻ formed inside red cells diffuses out into plasma [1]; Cl⁻ moves in to maintain electrical neutrality (balance of charge) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the Bohr shift is advantageous during exercise.
items.answer: Respiring muscles release more CO₂; haemoglobin releases more oxygen at the same pO₂ (lower affinity), supplying muscles with more O₂ for aerobic respiration.
items.markingKey: Respiring muscles release more CO₂ [1]; haemoglobin releases more oxygen at the same pO₂ (lower affinity) [1]; supplying muscles with more O₂ for aerobic respiration [1] [3]

items.stem: The table shows the percentage saturation of human haemoglobin with oxygen at different partial pressures of oxygen: 1 kPa: 4%, 2 kPa: 19%, 3 kPa: 42%, 4 kPa: 61%, 5 kPa: 74%, 6 kPa: 82%, 8 kPa: 91%, 10 kPa: 95%, 12 kPa: 97%, 13 kPa: 97%. Fully saturated blood carries 20.5 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³. (a) Using the data, calculate the volume of oxygen released per 100 cm³ of blood as it passes from the lungs (pO₂ 13 kPa) to a tissue with pO₂ 4 kPa.
items.answer: (a) 7.38 cm³

items.stem: The table shows the percentage saturation of human haemoglobin with oxygen at different partial pressures of oxygen: 1 kPa: 4%, 2 kPa: 19%, 3 kPa: 42%, 4 kPa: 61%, 5 kPa: 74%, 6 kPa: 82%, 8 kPa: 91%, 10 kPa: 95%, 12 kPa: 97%, 13 kPa: 97%. Fully saturated blood carries 20 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³. (a) Using the data, calculate the volume of oxygen released per 100 cm³ of blood as it passes from the lungs (pO₂ 13 kPa) to a tissue with pO₂ 2 kPa. (b) During exercise the carbon dioxide concentration in the tissue rises and the saturation at 2 kPa falls to 12%. Name this effect and calculate the extra oxygen released per 100 cm³ (assume the lung saturation is 95%).
items.answer: (a) 15.6 cm³ (b) The Bohr shift; extra = 1 cm³

items.stem: The table shows the percentage saturation of human haemoglobin with oxygen at different partial pressures of oxygen: 1 kPa: 4%, 2 kPa: 19%, 3 kPa: 42%, 4 kPa: 61%, 5 kPa: 74%, 6 kPa: 82%, 8 kPa: 91%, 10 kPa: 95%, 12 kPa: 97%, 13 kPa: 97%. Fully saturated blood carries 20.5 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³. (a) Using the data, calculate the volume of oxygen released per 100 cm³ of blood as it passes from the lungs (pO₂ 13 kPa) to a tissue with pO₂ 2 kPa. (b) During exercise the carbon dioxide concentration in the tissue rises and the saturation at 2 kPa falls to 10%. Name this effect and calculate the extra oxygen released per 100 cm³ (assume the lung saturation is 94%). (c) Explain how a high carbon dioxide concentration causes haemoglobin to release more oxygen.
items.answer: (a) 15.99 cm³ (b) The Bohr shift; extra = 1.23 cm³ (c) CO₂ diffuses into red cells and forms carbonic acid (carbonic anhydrase), which dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; H⁺ binds to haemoglobin, forming haemoglobinic acid and changing its shape, lowering its affinity for oxygen.
items.markingKey: (a) saturation falls from 97% to 19% [1]; (97 − 19) ÷ 100 × 20.5 = 15.99 cm³ [1] (b) Bohr shift [1]; (94 − 10) ÷ 100 × 20.5 = 17.22; − 15.99 = 1.23 cm³ [2] (c) carbonic anhydrase / carbonic acid [1]; H⁺ released [1]; H⁺ binds Hb, lowers affinity [1] [8]

items.stem: Biologists in Bogotá compared the oxygen dissociation curve of the haemoglobin of a llama living high in the Andes with that of adult human haemoglobin. The curve for a llama living high in the Andes lies to the left of the human curve. (a) Explain what this tells you about the affinity of this haemoglobin for oxygen. (b) Suggest why this is an advantage to the organism.
items.answer: (a) Higher affinity (left) – more saturated at a given pO₂. (b) Can load oxygen at low pO₂ (high altitude / placenta / mud).
items.markingKey: (a) Higher affinity (left) – more saturated at a given pO₂ [2] [2] (b) Can load oxygen at low pO₂ (high altitude / placenta / mud) [2] [2]

items.stem: Biologists in Lagos compared the oxygen dissociation curve of the haemoglobin of a small mammal with a high metabolic rate, such as a shrew with that of adult human haemoglobin. The curve for a small mammal with a high metabolic rate, such as a shrew lies to the right of the human curve. (a) Suggest why this is an advantage to the organism. (b) Describe how carbon dioxide is transported from respiring tissues to the lungs.
items.answer: (a) Oxygen is unloaded more readily to tissues with a high respiration rate. (b) Mostly as HCO₃⁻ in plasma (carbonic anhydrase in red cells, chloride shift); some as carbaminohaemoglobin; some dissolved.
items.markingKey: (a) Oxygen is unloaded more readily to tissues with a high respiration rate [2] [2] (b) Mostly as HCO₃⁻ in plasma (carbonic anhydrase in red cells, chloride shift) [1]; some as carbaminohaemoglobin [1]; some dissolved [1] [3]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "oxyhaemoglobin"?
options: The enzyme in red blood cells that catalyses the reaction of carbon dioxide with water to form carbonic acid.
A measure of the concentration of oxygen in a mixture of gases or a solution, measured in kPa.
The decrease in the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen at high carbon dioxide concentrations, shifting the dissociation curve to the right.
items.answer: Haemoglobin combined with oxygen.
items.markingKey: Oxyhaemoglobin: haemoglobin combined with oxygen.

items.stem: Why is the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin S-shaped (sigmoid)?
options: Oxygen is very soluble in plasma
Binding of the first oxygen changes the shape of haemoglobin, making it easier for further oxygen molecules to bind
Haemoglobin has only one haem group
items.answer: Binding of the first oxygen changes the shape of haemoglobin, making it easier for further oxygen molecules to bind
items.markingKey: Cooperative binding.

items.stem: Explain why carbon monoxide is dangerous.
items.answer: It binds to haem far more strongly than oxygen (forming carboxyhaemoglobin), so less oxygen is carried; binding is almost irreversible.
items.markingKey: It binds to haem far more strongly than oxygen (forming carboxyhaemoglobin), so less oxygen is carried [1]; binding is almost irreversible [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how oxygen and carbon dioxide are transported in the blood and explain the significance of the Bohr shift.
items.answer: Hb with 4 haem / Fe²⁺, binds 4 O₂ cooperatively, sigmoid curve, loading at high pO₂ in lungs and unloading in tissues. CO₂: dissolved, carbaminohaemoglobin, mostly HCO₃⁻ via carbonic anhydrase, chloride shift, H⁺ buffered by Hb. Bohr shift: high CO₂ lowers affinity, more O₂ released in active tissues.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "systole"?
options: The contraction phase of the heart muscle.
Valves at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery that prevent backflow into the ventricles.
The relaxation phase of the heart muscle.
Valves between the atria and ventricles (tricuspid and bicuspid/mitral) that prevent backflow into the atria when the ventricles contract.
items.answer: The contraction phase of the heart muscle.
items.markingKey: Systole: the contraction phase of the heart muscle.

items.stem: Describe the pressure changes and valve movements in the left side of the heart during one cardiac cycle.
items.answer: Atrial systole: atrial pressure rises slightly, AV valve open, ventricle fills. Ventricular systole: ventricular pressure rises above atrial, AV valve closes; above aortic, semilunar valve opens, blood ejected. Diastole: ventricular pressure falls below aortic, semilunar valve closes; below atrial, AV valve opens.
items.markingKey: Atrial systole: atrial pressure rises slightly, AV valve open, ventricle fills [1]; Ventricular systole: ventricular pressure rises above atrial, AV valve closes [1]; above aortic, semilunar valve opens, blood ejected [1]; Diastole: ventricular pressure falls below aortic, semilunar valve closes [1]; below atrial, AV valve opens [1] [5]

items.stem: Explain why the pressure in the aorta never falls to zero.
items.answer: Elastic recoil of the aortic wall during diastole maintains pressure; semilunar valves prevent backflow.
items.markingKey: Elastic recoil of the aortic wall during diastole maintains pressure [1]; semilunar valves prevent backflow [1] [2]

items.stem: A cardiologist in Lima examines a patient with a leaking (incompetent) bicuspid valve. (a) Explain how this condition reduces the efficiency of the heart. (b) Explain why the left ventricle wall is thicker than the right.
items.answer: (a) Blood flows back into the left atrium during ventricular systole, so less blood is pumped into the aorta. (b) It pumps blood at higher pressure through the whole systemic circulation.

items.stem: When do the atrioventricular valves close?
options: When the pressure in the atria rises above the pressure in the ventricles
When pressure in the aorta exceeds that in the ventricle
When the pressure in the ventricles rises above the pressure in the atria
items.answer: When the pressure in the ventricles rises above the pressure in the atria

items.stem: Explain why the atrial walls are thinner than the ventricular walls.
items.answer: Atria pump blood only into the ventricles, a short distance at low pressure.

items.stem: Daniel writes in a revision note: "The right ventricle pumps less blood than the left because its wall is thinner." Identify the error and write a correct statement.

items.stem: In a pressure trace from the left side of the heart of a person in Toronto, at 0.2 s the ventricular pressure rises above the atrial pressure; at 0.25 s it rises above the aortic pressure (about 10.5 kPa); the ventricular pressure peaks at 17.1 kPa and the aortic pressure peaks at 16.5 kPa; at 0.55 s the ventricular pressure falls below the aortic pressure. items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "atrioventricular septum"?
options: A band of non-conducting fibrous tissue that stops excitation spreading directly from atria to ventricles.
The pacemaker: a patch of muscle in the wall of the right atrium that initiates each heartbeat by sending out waves of excitation.
A patch of tissue in the septum that delays the wave of excitation by about 0.1 s before passing it to the Purkyne tissue.
Specialised muscle fibres in the septum (bundle of His) and ventricle walls that conduct excitation rapidly to the base (apex) of the ventricles.
items.answer: A band of non-conducting fibrous tissue that stops excitation spreading directly from atria to ventricles.
items.markingKey: Atrioventricular septum: a band of non-conducting fibrous tissue that stops excitation spreading directly from atria to ventricles.

items.stem: Explain why the wave of excitation cannot pass directly from the atria to the ventricles.

items.stem: Compare the structure of a capillary and an artery, and relate each difference to the function of the vessel.
items.answer: Capillary: wall one cell thick (endothelium only), with gaps between cells; lumen about 7 μm, just wide enough for a red blood cell; it allows exchange of substances between blood and tissue fluid over a short diffusion distance. Artery: thick wall with much elastic tissue and smooth muscle; narrow lumen; no valves (except at the base of the aorta and pulmonary artery); it carries blood away from the heart at high pressure; elastic recoil smooths flow.
items.markingKey: three structural differences [3]; each linked to function [1] [4]

items.stem: A doctor in Lima sees a patient with swollen ankles (oedema) caused by long periods of sitting still on a flight. (a) Describe how tissue fluid is normally formed. (b) Explain how valves in veins help return blood to the heart.
items.answer: (a) High hydrostatic pressure at arterial end forces water and small solutes out through capillary walls; proteins and cells stay in blood. (b) Contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes veins; valves allow flow only towards the heart, preventing backflow.

items.stem: A cardiologist in Kathmandu examines a patient with a narrowed (stenosed) aortic semilunar valve. (a) Describe the normal sequence of events in one cardiac cycle. (b) Explain how this condition reduces the efficiency of the heart. (c) Explain why heart valves are needed.
items.answer: (a) Atrial systole (ventricles fill); ventricular systole (AV valves close, semilunar open, ejection); diastole (semilunar close, AV open, atria and ventricles fill). (b) The ventricle must generate a higher pressure to eject blood through the narrow opening; less blood ejected; heart muscle thickens. (c) To keep blood flowing in one direction / prevent backflow when pressure changes.
